compass.e: From Middle English compas (“a circle, circuit, limit, form, a mathematical instrument”), from Old French compas, from Medieval Latin compassus (“a circle, a circuit”), from Latin com- (“together”) + passus (“a pace, step, later a pass, way, route”); see pass, pace.

s.d: navigational instrument for finding directions
an area in which something acts or operates or has power or control:
x: a piano has a greater range than the human voice
the ambit of municipal legislation

s.d: the limit of capability
x: within the compass of education

s.d: drafting instrument used for drawing circles
A magnetic or electronic device used to determine the cardinal directions (usually magnetic or true north).
x: [H]ow many Seas to our fore-fathers impaſſable, for want of the Compaſſe?

1689/1690, John Locke, On improvement of understanding
He that […] first discovered the use of the compass […] did more for the propagation of knowledge […] than those who built workhouses.

s.d: A pair of compasses (a device used to draw circular arcs and transfer length measurements).
x: to fix one foot of their compass wherever they please

s.d: The range of notes of a musical instrument or voice.
x: You would sound me from my lowest note to the top of my compass.

s.d: (obsolete) A space within limits; an area.
x: In going up the Missisippi ^([sic]), we meet with nothing remarkable before we come to the Detour aux Anglois, the English Reach: in that part the river takes a large compass.
Animals, in their generation, are wiser than the sons of men but their wisdom is confined to a few particulars, and lies in a very narrow compass.

s.d: (obsolete) An enclosing limit; a boundary, a circumference.
x: within the compass of an encircling wall

s.d: Moderate bounds, limits of truth; moderation; due limits; used with within.
x: In two hundred years before (I speak within compass), no such commission had been executed.
"Saints!" she cried, "but what a noise you keep! Can you not speak in compass?"

s.d: (formal) Synonym of scope.
x: the compass of his argument
There is a truth and falsehood in all propositions on this subject, and a truth and falsehood, which lie not beyond the compass of human understanding.

s.d: (obsolete) Range, reach.
(obsolete) A passing round; circuit; circuitous course.
x: This day I breathed first; time is come round, / And where I did begin, there shall I end; / My life is run his compass.
They fetched a compass of seven days' journey.

s.d: A curved circular form.
bring about; accomplish
x: This writer attempts more than his talents can compass

s.d: travel around, either by plane or ship
x: We compassed the earth

s.d: get the meaning of something
x: Do you comprehend the meaning of this letter?

s.d: To surround; to encircle; to environ; to stretch round.
x:
Now all the blessings
Of a glad father compass thee about!
And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.

s.d: To go about or round entirely; to traverse.
x: So she goeth around the hill compassing.

s.d: (dated) To accomplish; to reach; to achieve; to obtain.
x: […] tho' theſe ſeem'd to be very unfit Inſtruments for compaſſing of that great Deſign for which they were then employ'd, becauſe of their Inability and Uncapacity in performing the Work ſo very great and important; […]
[...] they never find ways sufficient to compass that end.

s.d: (dated) To plot; to scheme (against someone).
x: That he plotted and compassed to raise Sedition and Rebellion [...]
But it went beyond it by the loose construction of compassing to depose the King, …

s.d: (obsolete) In a circuit; round about.
x: [T]he Towne is impailed about halfe a mile compaſſe.
Near the same plot of ground, for about six yards compasse were digged up coals and incinerated substances, […]

s.d: compass in the form of a card that rotates so that 0 degrees or North points to magnetic north
The circular card attached to the needles of a mariner's compass, on which are marked the thirty-two points or rhumbs.
any of several plants having leaves so arranged on the axis as to indicate the cardinal points of the compass
the direction in which a compass needle points
a plane with a flexible face that can plane concave or convex surfaces
A plane, convex in the direction of its length on the underside, for smoothing the concave faces of curved woodwork.
North American annual with red or rose-colored flowers
any of several plants having leaves so arranged on the axis as to indicate the cardinal points of the compass
Any of several plants, the leaves of which become oriented to the morning sun:: Lactuca serriola, native to Europe, widely introduced to temperate regions.
Any of several plants, the leaves of which become oriented to the morning sun:: Silphium laciniatum, native to eastern North America.
any of 32 horizontal directions indicated on the card of a compass
x: he checked the point on his compass

s.d: Any of the horizontal directions indicated on a compass. There may be 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, or even 128 compass points on a compass, depending on its size and accuracy.
a handsaw with a narrow triangular blade for cutting curves
A saw that cuts in a circular manner.

compassion.e: From Middle English compassioun, compassion, from Old French compassion, from Ecclesiastical Latin compassio (“sympathy”), from Latin compati, past participle compassus (“to suffer together with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion. By surface analysis, com- + passion.

s.d: a deep awareness of and sympathy for another's suffering
the humane quality of understanding the suffering of others and wanting to do something about it
(uncountable) Deep awareness of the suffering of others that people have to the point of them being motivated to relieve such states.
x: Oh! the unspeakable privilege to have Him for our Father, who is the Father of mercies and compassions, and those not barren, fruitless pityings, for He is withal the God of all consolations.
Other people's problems, they overwhelm my mind / They say compassion is a virtue, but I don't have the time

s.d: (obsolete) To pity.
x: O heavens, can you hear a good man groan / And not relent, or not compassion him?
Both wanted in early life the one thing essential to every individual, of whatever nature or degree of intellect, a kind, compassioning adviser; - a true friend;[…].

compassionate.e: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.

s.d: share the suffering of
(archaic) To feel compassion (for someone or with regard to something); to regard (someone or something) with compassion.
x: […] seeing them die so wofully in the flames, he compassionated them.

The Justice which Mr. Allworthy had executed on Partridge, at first met with universal Approbation; but no sooner had he felt its Consequences, than his Neighbours began to relent, and to compassionate his Case;

s.d: showing or having compassion
x: heard the soft and compassionate voices of women

s.d: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).
x: The Compassionate, the All-Compassionate

As a compassionate Turcoyse which doth tell
By looking pale, the wearer is not well,

s.d: Given to someone as an exception because of a family emergency or a death in their family.
x: compassionate leave; a compassionate visa

s.d: (obsolete) Inviting or asking for pity.
x:
It boots thee not to be compassionate:
After our sentence plaining comes too late.

s.d: (military) leave granted in an emergency such as family sickness or death
(uncountable) A period of absence from work taken by an employee due to a personal matter, either illness or death.

[…] but Gwendolen, instead of any such symptoms as pallor and silence, had only deepened the compassionateness of her brow and eyes,

compatibility.e: Borrowed from New Latin compatibilitās. By surface analysis, compatible + -ity.

s.d: a feeling of sympathetic understanding
capability of existing or performing in harmonious or congenial combination
(uncountable) The state of being compatible; in which two or more things are able to exist or work together in combination without problems or conflict.
x: They will feature wider gangways for better wheelchair accessibility, as well as compatibility with platform screen doors - should these ever be introduced in the future.

s.d: (uncountable) the capability of two or more items or components of equipment or material to exist or function in the same system or environment without mutual interference.
(uncountable) the ability to execute a given program on different types of computers without modification of the program or the computers. See backward compatibility and forward compatibility.

(uncountable) the capability that allows the substitution of one subsystem (storage facility), or of one functional unit (e.g., hardware, software), for the originally designated system or functional unit in a relatively transparent manner, without loss of information and without the introduction of errors.
(uncountable) the continuity or good fit of material or members or components while being deformed.

compatible.e: Inherited from Middle English compatible, fron Anglo-Norman compatible, from Medieval Latin compatibilis (“in compatibile beneficium, a benefice which could be held together with another one”), from Late Latin compator (“to suffer with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion.

s.d: Something that is compatible with something else.
x: a computer company that sells IBM compatibles

s.d: able to exist and perform in harmonious or agreeable combination
x: a compatible married couple
her deeds were compatible with her ideology

s.d: capable of being used with or connected to other devices or components without modification
capable of forming a homogeneous mixture that neither separates nor is altered by chemical interaction
Capable of working together without conflict.
x: This printer isn't compatible with my computer.

s.d: Able to get along well.
x: My neighbours and I are not very compatible: they're loud and I'm an introvert.

s.d: Consistent; congruous.
x: His actions were compatible with his sermons.
She was like a Beardsley Salome, he had said. And indeed she had the narrow eyes and the high cheekbone of that creature, and as nearly the sinuosity as is compatible with human symmetry.

s.d: application software programs that share common conventions so they can be utilized together
software that can run on different computers without modification

s.d: with compatibility

compatriot.e: Borrowed from French compatriote, itself borrowed from Latin compatriota. By surface analysis, com- + patriot. Displaced native Old English ġelanda.

s.d: a person from your own country
Somebody from one's own country.
x: the distrust with which they felt themselves to be regarded by their compatriots in America
However Russian Pavlyuchenko stunned his compatriots with an unstoppable 25-yard drive into the top corner.

s.d: Of the same country; especially, being countrymen and having a common sentiment of patriotism.
x: She [Britain] rears to Freedom an undaunted Race: / Compatriot zealous, hoſpitable, kind, […]

compeer.e: From Middle English comper, from Middle French comper, from Latin compater, compatrem. Doublet of compere as well as compadre and goombah. Influenced by folk-etymological analysis as com- + peer.

s.d: a person who is of equal standing with another in a group
(obsolete) The equal or peer of someone else; a close companion or associate.
x: And him thus answer'd soon his bold compeer.
She had fallen into the common error of supposing that the author must personify his works, and that his conversation must be copy and compeer of his writings.

s.d: To be equal with; to match.
x: In my rights, / By me invested, he compeers the best.

s.d: necessitate or exact
x: the water shortage compels conservation

s.d: (archaic) To drive together, round up.
x: The shepherds compelled the stray sheep into the fold as night began to fall.

s.d: To overpower; to subdue.
x: She had one of those perfect faces, which irresistibly compel the soul of a man.

s.d: To force, constrain, or coerce.
x: Logic compels the wise, while fools feel compelled by emotions.
Congratulations, your courage compels respect.

s.d: To forcefully or powerfully motivate (a course of action).
x: As the novel progresses, it picks up a propulsive energy, the kind that compels you to keep reading straight through to the end.

s.d: To have a strong, irresistible force (on someone or something).
To exact, extort, (make) produce by force.
x: Commissions, which compel from each / The sixth part of his substance.
The Queen has nothing but the power to execute the laws, to adjust grievances and to compel order.

s.d: (obsolete) To force to yield; to overpower; to subjugate.
x: Easy sleep their weary limbs compell'd.
And I will fetch you forage from all fields, / For I compel all creatures to my will.

s.d: (obsolete) To gather or unite in a crowd or company.
x: in one troop compell'd

s.d: (obsolete) To call forth; to summon.
x: She had this knight from far compeld.
the pow'rs that I compel / Shall throw thee hence, and make thy head run ope the gates of hel

s.d: An act of compulsion; an obliging somebody to do something.
driving or forcing
x: compelling ambition

s.d: tending to persuade by forcefulness of argument
x: new and compelling evidence

s.d: very interesting; able to capture and hold one's attention
x: The novel was so compelling that I couldn't put it down.

s.d: capable of causing someone to believe or agree
x: He made a compelling argument.

Terry's goal looked to have put Chelsea in control on the stroke of half-time but Arsenal's response presented a compelling case for Wenger's insistence that reports of his side's demise have been greatly exaggerated.

s.d: strong and forceful; that causes one to feel like they must do something
x: I would need a very compelling reason to leave my job.

compendious.e: From Old French compendieux, from Latin compendiosus (“advantageous, abridged, brief”), from compendium.

s.d: briefly giving the gist of something
x: a short and compendious book
a compact style is brief and pithy

s.d: containing a subset of words, succinctly described; abridged and summarized
briefly describing a body of knowledge

compendium.e: From the Latin compendium (“that which is weighed together; a sparing, a saving, an abbreviation”), from com- (“with”) + pendō (“to weigh”).

s.d: a publication containing a variety of works
a concise but comprehensive summary of a larger work
A short, complete summary; an abstract.
A list or collection of various items.
x: It was this last variety which formed the backbone of the first published Italian compendium of games, Innocenzo Ringhieri's One Hundred Games of Liberality and Ingenuity of 1551, dedicated to Cathérine de' Medici.

s.d: A list or collection of various items.: A collection of board games packaged in a single box.
A list or collection of various items.: A collected body of information on the standards of strength, purity, and quality of drugs.

compensable.e: Borrowed from French compensable; by surface analysis, compens(ate) + -able.

s.d: That which is eligible for compensation.
for which money is paid
x: a paying job
remunerative work

s.d: Able to be compensated.
Entitling one to compensation.
x: compensable disease
Coalworker's pneumoconiosis is a compensable disease in various countries, and it is a preventable disease where the costs of its prevention are not shirked as externalities.

compensate.e: Borrowed from Latin compēnsātus, perfect passive participle of compensō (“to weight together one thing against another, balance, make good”), -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.

s.d: adjust for
x: engineers will work to correct the effects of air resistance

s.d: make amends for; pay compensation for
x: One can never fully repair the suffering and losses of the Jews in the Third Reich
She was compensated for the loss of her arm in the accident

s.d: make up for shortcomings or a feeling of inferiority by exaggerating good qualities
x: he is compensating for being a bad father

s.d: make reparations or amends for
x: right a wrong done to the victims of the Holocaust

s.d: do or give something to somebody in return
x: Does she pay you for the work you are doing?

s.d: make payment to; compensate
x: My efforts were not remunerated

s.d: To do (something good) after (something bad) happens.
To pay or reward someone in exchange for work done or some other consideration.
x: It is hard work, but they will compensate you well for it.

s.d: To make up for; to do something in place of something else; to correct, satisfy; to reach an agreement such that the scales are literally or (metaphorically) balanced; to equalize or make even.
x: His loud voice cannot compensate for a lack of personality.
To compensate me for his tree landing on my shed, my neighbor paved my driveway.

s.d: To adjust or adapt to a change, often a harm or deprivation.
x: I hate that old car because it steers a little to the left and I'm always compensating for that when I drive it.
To compensate for his broken leg, Gary uses crutches.

s.d: receiving or eligible for compensation
x: salaried workers
a stipendiary magistrate

s.d: That received compensation (payment)
x: Some commenters foresaw the possibility that "a handful of very compensated employees could tilt the average high enough to meet the minimum average benefit with little or no contributions to the 'average' employee .

s.d: That has been adjusted to compensate for some circumstances.
x: But, if my view is correct, the only gold standard which could have survived during the last few years would have been the very compensated gold dollar against which the bankers' report was written.

s.d: a minimum credit balance that a bank may require a borrower to keep on deposit as a condition for granting a loan; a common requirement for establishing a line of credit at a bank
x: the compensating balance increases the effective interest rate to the bank since the net amount loaned is reduced but the interest paid is unchanged

compensation.e: From Middle English compensacioun, from Old French compensacion, from Latin compensātiōnem, accusative singular of compensātiō. Equivalent to compensate + -ion.

s.d: something (such as money) given or received as payment or reparation (as for a service or loss or injury)
(psychiatry) a defense mechanism that conceals your undesirable shortcomings by exaggerating desirable behaviors
the act of compensating for service or loss or injury
(uncountable) The act or principle of compensating.
x: Human labor, through all its forms, from the sharpening of a stake to the construction of a city or an epic, is one immense illustration of the perfect compensation of the universe.

s.d: (uncountable) Something which is regarded as an equivalent; something which compensates for loss.
x: The parliament which dissolved the monastic foundations […] vouchsafed not a word toward securing the slightest compensation to the dispossessed owners.
No pecuniary compensation can possibly reward them.

s.d: (uncountable) The extinction of debts of which two persons are reciprocally debtors by the credits of which they are reciprocally creditors; the payment of a debt by a credit of equal amount.
(uncountable) A recompense or reward for service.

(uncountable) An equivalent stipulated for in contracts for the sale of real estate, in which it is customary to provide that errors in description, etc., shall not avoid, but shall be the subject of compensation.

(uncountable) The relationship between air temperature outside a building and a calculated target temperature for provision of air or water to contained rooms or spaces for the purpose of efficient heating. In building control systems, the compensation curve is defined to a compensator for this purpose.
(uncountable) The ability of one part of the brain to overfunction in order to take over the function of a damaged part (e.g. following a stroke).
an exchange in which an exporter receives goods from an importer as a part of the payment.
(law) compensation for losses that can readily be proven to have occurred and for which the injured party has the right to be compensated
spending money raised by borrowing; used by governments to stimulate their economy
time off that is granted to a worker as compensation for working overtime
(uncountable) Synonym of comp time.

compere.e: A borrowing of French compère (“partner, accomplice”), from Old French comper, from Late Latin compater (“godfather”), from Latin com- (“with”) + pater (“father”). Doublet of compeer, compadre, and goombah.

s.d: British term for someone who introduces television acts or cabarets etc
(Ireland, UK) A master of ceremonies, especially for a television, variety, or quiz show.
x: Every year I am the compere for our Church Quiz Night.
The compere came onto the stage holding the gold envelope that contained the winner's name.

s.d: act as a master of ceremonies
To emcee, to act as compere.
x: I will be compering for next week's Village Fete.

compete.e: Borrowed from Middle French competer, from Latin competere (“to coincide, to be equal to, to be capable of”), from com- (“with”) + petō (“to seek; to aim for, strive for”). Compare Latin competītor (“competitor”).

s.d: compete for something; engage in a contest; measure oneself against others
To be in battle or in a rivalry with another for the same thing, position, or reward; to contend.
x: The idea behind Sir Montagu's gift is that there should be for the amateur clubs a trophy which will take the place of the Stanley Cup, now becoming a trophy for which professional clubs will alone compete.

s.d: To be in a position in which it is possible to win or triumph.
To take part in a contest, game or similar event.
To strive to achieve or obtain something which another also strives for, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

competence.e: Borrowed from Middle French compétence, from Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competency.

s.d: the quality of being adequately or well qualified physically and intellectually
(uncountable) The quality or state of being competent, i.e. able or suitable for a general role.
x: Teachers are now required to teach intercultural communicative competence.

s.d: (uncountable) The system of linguistic knowledge possessed by native speakers of a language, as opposed to its actual use in concrete situations (performance), cf. linguistic competence.
(dated, uncountable) A sustainable income.
x: Reason's whole pleasure, all the joys of sense, / Lie in three words — health, peace, and competence.
“money can only give happiness where there is nothing else to give it. Beyond a competence, it can afford no real satisfaction, as far as mere self is concerned.”

s.d: the legal authority to deal with a matter.
x: The bill was denied royal assent because the Scottish Parliament does not have legislative competence on the bill's matter.

K C Wheare's definition of federalism requires that two governments be independent and co-ordinate within their own spheres, generally set out by the division of competences codified in a constitution, which is supreme.

s.d: (uncountable) The degree to which a rock is resistant to deformation or flow.
a hearing to determine legal capacity (to determine whether the defendant can understand the charges and cooperate with a lawyer in preparing a defense)

competency.e: From Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competence.

s.d: the quality of being adequately or well qualified physically and intellectually
(uncountable) The ability to perform some task; competence.
x: The loan demonstrates, in regard to instrumental resources, the competency of this kingdom to the assertion of the common cause.
What professional competencies do science teachers need?

s.d: (uncountable) An individual's capacity to understand the nature and implications of their legal rights and obligations.
(uncountable) Implicit knowledge of a language’s structure.
(obsolete, uncountable) A sufficient supply of something.
x: the next day they returned unsuspected, leaving their confederates to follow, and in the interim, to convay them a competencie of all things they could […]
[…] it would appear that before taking this precaution Mr. Bree must have had the thrift to remove a modest competency of the gold […]

s.d: (obsolete, uncountable) A sustainable income.
x: Superfluity comes sooner by white hairs, but competency lives longer.
And that knights competency you haue gotten / VVith care and labour: he vvith luſt and idleneſſe / VVill bring into the ſtypend of a begger; […]

competent.e: From Middle English competent, conpetent, from Old French competent (modern French compétent), from Latin competens, competentem, present participle of competō (“coincide, be equal to, be capable of”). Compare Dutch competent (“competent”), German kompetent (“competent”), Danish kompetent (“competent”).

s.d: A catechumen selected for baptism.
properly or sufficiently qualified or capable or efficient
x: a competent typist

s.d: adequate, but not outstanding or exceptional
x: a competent performance

s.d: legally qualified or sufficient
x: a competent court
competent testimony

s.d: Having sufficient skill, knowledge, ability, or qualifications.
x: He is a competent skier and an expert snowboarder.
I believe in that myself because it has been explained by competent men as the convolutions of the grey matter.

s.d: Having jurisdiction or authority over a particular issue or question.
x: For any disagreements arising from this contract, the competent court shall be the Springfield Circuit Court.
judicial authority having competent jurisdiction

s.d: an abstract or general idea inferred or derived from specific instances
Something constructed from parts.
x: The artwork was a construct of wire and tubes.
Loops and conditional statements are constructs in computer programming.

s.d: A concept or model.
x: Bohr's theoretical construct of the atom was soon superseded by quantum mechanics.

s.d: A segment of nucleic acid, created artificially, for transplantation into a target cell or tissue.
make by combining materials and parts
x: this little pig made his house out of straw

s.d: put together out of artificial or natural components or parts
x: the company fabricates plastic chairs
They manufacture small toys

s.d: draw with suitable instruments and under specified conditions
x: construct an equilateral triangle

s.d: create by linking linguistic units
x: construct a sentence
construct a paragraph

s.d: create by organizing and linking ideas, arguments, or concepts
x: construct a proof
construct an argument

s.d: reassemble mentally
x: reconstruct the events of 20 years ago

s.d: To build or form (something) by assembling parts.
x: We constructed the radio from spares.

x: A sentence may be constructed with a subject, verb and object.
The Vietnam War films are forms of memory that function to provide collective rememberings, to construct history, and to subsume within them the experience of the veterans.

s.d: To draw (a geometric figure) by following precise specifications and using geometric tools and techniques.
x: Construct a circle that touches each vertex of the given triangle.
The arc of a circle may be very little, but, given that, it is possible to construct the entire figure.

s.d: a new writing system specifically created by an individual or group, rather than having evolved as part of a language or culture like a natural script.
x: Balin-Silel is a constructed script invented by Aayush Chaturvedi in November 2014 to write his conlang by the same name.

his hobby was the building of boats

s.d: a group of words that form a constituent of a sentence and are considered as a single unit

a thing constructed; a complex entity constructed of many parts
x: the structure consisted of a series of arches

s.d: drawing a figure satisfying certain conditions as part of solving a problem or proving a theorem

s.d: (uncountable) A (usually non-representational) structure, such as a collage etc.

s.d: (uncountable) The manner in which something is built.
x: A thing of simple construction.

s.d: (uncountable) A group of words arranged to form a meaningful phrase.

s.d: (uncountable) The meaning or interpretation of a text, action etc.; the way something is viewed by an observer or onlooker.

Customary; considered law by virtue of the fact that it is generally observed.

Both we will raigne as Conſuls of the earth,

 Are at the Dukes already.
